meta_description_en: Bryan Russell explores English slang, idioms, and synonyms for drunkenness, recounting the only time in his life he had a drink before starting his National Service.
meta_description_ru: Брайан Рассел исследует английские синонимы и сленг, обозначающие опьянение, и вспоминает единственный случай из своей жизни накануне армейской службы.
body_en_plain:
A DISSERTATION ON DRUNKEN-
   NESS     By Bryan Russell
   --------------------------
Unlike the vast majority of men
(and most women too) I have
never been greatly interested in
the consumption of alcoholic
liquor. One reason for this is
probably that my first job was
with a beer bottling firm and
although I worked in the office
department, the smell of the
stuff permeated the whole prem-
ises and although one got used
to this ubiquitous odour it was
never pleasant.

When I was 21 I joined the Salv-
ation Army, all members of which
have to be total abstainers from
alcohol. I kept this pledge
faithfully until I left the org-
anisation some ten years later
but very rarely visit a public
house or drink beer, wine or
spirits. Not because I think
there is anything wrong with
that; it simply does not inter-
est me. So I have never been
drunk. Except for just possibly
once in my life. I have,however,
been fascinated by the large
number of synonyms and altern-
ative phrases for the state of
body and mind caused by the
imbibing of an excessive amount
of alcohol: amusing, graphic,
ridiculous and some quite inex-
plicable.

The two official adjectives are
inebriated and intoxicated. The
former refers to the actual
state of drunkenness; the latter
more particularly to the poison-
ous quality of alcohol.


A Victorian gentleman who had
drunk too much was said to be
'In his cups'; perhaps referring
to the stirrup cup from which
everyone partook freely before
the hunt set off.


Another polite term was 'Under
the weather', once used exclus-
ively of drunkenness, now gener-
ally applied to anyone feeling
below par.


For slightly or moderately drunk
read 'merry', (for the false
sense of elation); 'tipsy' or
'fuddled' (to describe the state
of mind). 'Obfuscated' (which
sounds slightly vulgar) being
the correct term.

'One over the eight' is an
interesting one, based on the
myth that one could take eight
drinks and remain sober but nine
drinks took you into the realms
of drunkenness. Of course the
size of the glass and the alco-
holic quality of the contents
would have much to do with it. I
doubt very much that eight
glasses of the mildest tipple,
e.g. shandy, would get you past
the breathalyzer test.


'Tight' is quite old-fashioned
and probably never used now. I'm
not sure of the meaning of this
one. 'Loose' would be a more
appropriate word I would have
thought.

'Canned' is a more modern term
perhaps arising from the sale of
liquor in cans rather than
bottles. While 'Blotto' (not in
the dictionary) might have
something to do with soaking up
alcohol as blotting paper soaks
up ink.

'Tanked' or 'Tanked up' is a
'laddish' term and much more
common today. It may possibly
have some connection with
'canned' or perhaps refers to


the consumption of a whole
'tankful' of alcohol or even the
motorised 'tanker' in which the
stuff is delivered in bulk. (or
used to be when I was in that
trade).


Of course there are many words
like 'sloshed' and 'smashed'
which simply refer to the
disintegration of personality
caused by drunkenness which some
people still find excruciatingly
funny. 'Stoned out of ones mind'
also comes in this category but
having used it in 'Dark Side of
the Moon' I was told the term
referred more properly to drugs
than alcohol and would be
anachronistic in 2000.


The cockney word for drunkenness
is BRAHMS ('Brahms and Liszt')
and Liszt rhymes with... well,
you all know what it rhymes
with!

Other words for seriously drunk
are 'Paralytic' , 'Blind Drunk'
and 'Dead Drunk' which are
self-explanatory. An interesting
word in this context is'Sozzled'
a dialect word meaning 'to mix
sloppily' which could describe
the behaviour of the drunkard or
the preparation of the drinks
that brought him to such a
state.

'Lit-up' probably refers to the
alcoholic glow on the features
of someone who had drink more


than they ought to; 'Pie-eyed'
is an amusing description of the
blank,staring look of someone in
a similar state of inebriation.
This was adequately demonstrated
for me by a photograph of the
England soccer team at a drunken
binge in Hong-Kong. Paul
Gascoigne and Teddy Sherringham
were definitely 'pie-eyed.'


'Pickled' probably refers to the
confused state of mind of the
imbiber, like 'sloshed' or
'smashed' while 'Stinko' or
'Stinking' derives from the
unpleasant smell of alcohol on
the drunkards breath or cloth-
ing.


The aforementioned terms were
all used by Hubert Gregg who in
1944 wrote a song about the kind
of celebration he was going to
have when the war ended. It was
called 'I'm Going to Get Lit-up
When the Lights Go Up in London'
and each verse contained a
different word or phrase to
describe the same thing e.g.,
'I'm Going to get Pie-eyed....'
'I'm Going to get Pickled....
'I'm Going to get Stinking.....'
etc. etc.

The song proved to be very popu-
lar and questions in the House
of Commons were even raised. The
abstemious Lady Astor was con-
cerned that Mr. Gregg's exhorta-
tion might encourage 'wholesale
unbridled debauchery' to which

Winston Churchill replied
(probably with tongue in cheek)
'I'm sure the British people
will show admirable restraint
while enjoying the occasion.

One thing more. I mentioned at
the beginning of this essay that
I might have been 'slightly
drunk' on just one occasion and
as you're probably dying to know
(or even if you're not) I shall
tell you that this auspicious
event took place on the night of
October 17th 1951. It was the
day before I began my ill-fated
National Service career and my
workmates took me along to a lo-
cal pub for a 'few drinks' which
was more or less traditional. It
was, after all, a beer-bottling
firm.

I can't say I enjoyed the occas-
ion very much but I remember
that the office manager and the
cashier consumed large quantit-
ies of Guinness and Brown Ale
and went home somewhat the worse
for wear. I suppose I had a few
Worthington Green Shields just
to be sociable and to dull my
mind about what awaited me on
the morrow.

When the proceedings were over
and everyone had dispersed nois-
ily down South Lambeth Road, one
of my colleagues,Freddie Clarke,
having not long completed his
own stint in the army, insisted
on accompanying me on the bus to
Camberwell and actually walking
with me to my door. It was very


gallant of him and when I asked
him why he was so disposed to
put himself out in this way he
simply commented 'Mustn't have
you late on parade tomorrow old
son' and walked off into the
darkness.

             Bryan Russell
.
body_en:
### A Dissertation on Drunkenness

**By Bryan Russell**

Unlike the vast majority of men (and most women too) I have never been greatly interested in the consumption of alcoholic liquor. One reason for this is probably that my first job was with a beer bottling firm and although I worked in the office department, the smell of the stuff permeated the whole premises and although one got used to this ubiquitous odour it was never pleasant.

When I was 21 I joined the Salvation Army, all members of which have to be total abstainers from alcohol. I kept this pledge faithfully until I left the organisation some ten years later but very rarely visit a public house or drink beer, wine or spirits. Not because I think there is anything wrong with that; it simply does not interest me. So I have never been drunk. Except for just possibly once in my life. I have, however, been fascinated by the large number of synonyms and alternative phrases for the state of body and mind caused by the imbibing of an excessive amount of alcohol: amusing, graphic, ridiculous and some quite inexplicable.

The two official adjectives are *inebriated* and *intoxicated*. The former refers to the actual state of drunkenness; the latter more particularly to the poisonous quality of alcohol.

A Victorian gentleman who had drunk too much was said to be 'In his cups'; perhaps referring to the stirrup cup from which everyone partook freely before the hunt set off.

Another polite term was 'Under the weather', once used exclusively of drunkenness, now generally applied to anyone feeling below par.

For slightly or moderately drunk read 'merry', (for the false sense of elation); 'tipsy' or 'fuddled' (to describe the state of mind). 'Obfuscated' (which sounds slightly vulgar) being the correct term.

'One over the eight' is an interesting one, based on the myth that one could take eight drinks and remain sober but nine drinks took you into the realms of drunkenness. Of course the size of the glass and the alcoholic quality of the contents would have much to do with it. I doubt very much that eight glasses of the mildest tipple, e.g. shandy, would get you past the breathalyzer test.

'Tight' is quite old-fashioned and probably never used now. I'm not sure of the meaning of this one. 'Loose' would be a more appropriate word I would have thought.

'Canned' is a more modern term perhaps arising from the sale of liquor in cans rather than bottles. While 'Blotto' (not in the dictionary) might have something to do with soaking up alcohol as blotting paper soaks up ink.

'Tanked' or 'Tanked up' is a 'laddish' term and much more common today. It may possibly have some connection with 'canned' or perhaps refers to the consumption of a whole 'tankful' of alcohol or even the motorised 'tanker' in which the stuff is delivered in bulk (or used to be when I was in that trade).

Of course there are many words like 'sloshed' and 'smashed' which simply refer to the disintegration of personality caused by drunkenness which some people still find excruciatingly funny. 'Stoned out of one's mind' also comes in this category but having used it in *Dark Side of the Moon* I was told the term referred more properly to drugs than alcohol and would be anachronistic in 2000.

The cockney word for drunkenness is BRAHMS ('Brahms and Liszt') and Liszt rhymes with... well, you all know what it rhymes with!

Other words for seriously drunk are 'Paralytic', 'Blind Drunk' and 'Dead Drunk' which are self-explanatory. An interesting word in this context is 'Sozzled', a dialect word meaning 'to mix sloppily' which could describe the behaviour of the drunkard or the preparation of the drinks that brought him to such a state.

'Lit-up' probably refers to the alcoholic glow on the features of someone who had drunk more than they ought to; 'Pie-eyed' is an amusing description of the blank, staring look of someone in a similar state of inebriation. This was adequately demonstrated for me by a photograph of the England soccer team at a drunken binge in Hong-Kong. Paul Gascoigne and Teddy Sherringham were definitely 'pie-eyed.'

'Pickled' probably refers to the confused state of mind of the imbiber, like 'sloshed' or 'smashed' while 'Stinko' or 'Stinking' derives from the unpleasant smell of alcohol on the drunkard's breath or clothing.

The aforementioned terms were all used by Hubert Gregg who in 1944 wrote a song about the kind of celebration he was going to have when the war ended. It was called *'I'm Going to Get Lit-up When the Lights Go Up in London'* and each verse contained a different word or phrase to describe the same thing, e.g., 'I'm Going to get Pie-eyed....', 'I'm Going to get Pickled....', 'I'm Going to get Stinking.....' etc. etc.

The song proved to be very popular and questions in the House of Commons were even raised. The abstemious Lady Astor was concerned that Mr. Gregg's exhortation might encourage 'wholesale unbridled debauchery' to which Winston Churchill replied (probably with tongue in cheek): 'I'm sure the British people will show admirable restraint while enjoying the occasion.'

One thing more. I mentioned at the beginning of this essay that I might have been 'slightly drunk' on just one occasion and as you're probably dying to know (or even if you're not) I shall tell you that this auspicious event took place on the night of October 17th 1951. It was the day before I began my ill-fated National Service career and my workmates took me along to a local pub for a 'few drinks' which was more or less traditional. It was, after all, a beer-bottling firm.

I can't say I enjoyed the occasion very much but I remember that the office manager and the cashier consumed large quantities of Guinness and Brown Ale and went home somewhat the worse for wear. I suppose I had a few Worthington Green Shields just to be sociable and to dull my mind about what awaited me on the morrow.

When the proceedings were over and everyone had dispersed noisily down South Lambeth Road, one of my colleagues, Freddie Clarke, having not long completed his own stint in the army, insisted on accompanying me on the bus to Camberwell and actually walking with me to my door. It was very gallant of him and when I asked him why he was so disposed to put himself out in this way he simply commented: 'Mustn't have you late on parade tomorrow, old son' and walked off into the darkness.

**Bryan Russell**
body_ru:
### Рассуждение о пьянстве

**Брайан Рассел**

В отличие от подавляющего большинства мужчин (да и большинства женщин тоже), я никогда особо не интересовался употреблением алкогольных напитков. Одна из причин, вероятно, кроется в том, что моя первая работа была на пиворазливочном предприятии. Хотя я работал в конторском отделе, запах этого варева пропитывал все помещения, и, хоть к этому вездесущему аромату и можно было привыкнуть, приятным он никогда не был.

Когда мне исполнился 21 год, я вступил в Армию Спасения, все члены которой обязаны быть абсолютными трезвенниками. Я свято держал эту клятву, пока не покинул организацию примерно десять лет спустя, но и потом крайне редко заходил в пабы или пил пиво, вино или крепкие напитки. Не потому, что считаю это чем-то предосудительным; мне это просто-напросто неинтересно. Так что пьяным я не был никогда. Ну, разве что один-единственный раз в жизни. Тем не менее меня всегда завораживало огромное количество синонимов и выражений, описывающих состояние тела и духа, вызванное чрезмерным возлиянием: забавных, образных, нелепых и порой совершенно необъяснимых.

Два официальных прилагательных — это *inebriated* («охмелевший») и *intoxicated* («одурманенный, отравленный алкоголем»). Первое описывает само состояние опьянения, второе же скорее указывает на токсические свойства спиртного.

Про викторианского джентльмена, выпившего лишнего, говорили: *«In his cups»* («в своих кубках / во хмелю»); возможно, это восходит к «стременной чаше», которую все охотно осушали перед началом охоты.

Другим вежливым выражением было *«Under the weather»* («не в своей тарелке»); когда-то оно использовалось исключительно применительно к пьяным, а сейчас обычно описывает любого человека, слегка приболевшего или чувствующего недомогание.

Для лёгкого или умеренного опьянения подойдут слова *«merry»* («навеселе», из-за ложного чувства эйфории), *«tipsy»* («под мухой») или *«fuddled»* («одурманенный», для описания помрачённого рассудка). Более книжным и строгим термином является *«obfuscated»* («помрачённый», хотя на слух воспринимается чуть ли не вульгарно).

*«One over the eight»* («лишняя рюмка сверх восьми») — любопытное выражение, основанное на мифе о том, будто можно выпить восемь порций и остаться трезвым, а вот девятая непременно заведёт вас в пучину опьянения. Разумеется, размер бокала и крепость напитка играют в этом не последнюю роль. Очень сомневаюсь, что даже восемь стаканов самого безобидного зелья, вроде шенди, позволят вам пройти тест на алкотестере.

Слово *«Tight»* («натянутый, тугой») звучит весьма старомодно и сегодня, пожалуй, уже не употребляется. Я, честно говоря, не совсем понимаю его смысл. Логичнее было бы использовать слово *«Loose»* («разболтанный, расслабленный»).

*«Canned»* («законсервированный / под банкой») — более современный термин, возникший, вероятно, с появлением спиртного в жестяных банках вместо бутылок. В то же время слово *«Blotto»* («в стельку», его нет в словаре), возможно, связано со способностью впитывать алкоголь так, как промокательная бумага впитывает чернила (*blotting paper*).

*«Tanked»* или *«Tanked up»* («заправившийся до краёв») — слово из молодёжного, пацанского сленга, ныне гораздо более распространённое. Возможно, оно имеет отношение к *«canned»*, а может, намекает на опустошение целой «цистерны» (*tank*) алкоголя или даже на автоцистерну (*tanker*), в которой напиток доставляют оптом (во всяком случае, так возили в те времена, когда я работал на разливочной фирме).

Разумеется, есть множество слов вроде *«sloshed»* («вдрызг») и *«smashed»* («в хлам»), которые прямо указывают на распад личности под воздействием зеленого змия — зрелище, которое некоторые до сих пор находят гомерически смешным. *«Stoned out of one's mind»* («одурманенный до потери памяти») тоже подходит к этой категории, однако когда я использовал его в *Dark Side of the Moon*, мне сказали, что этот термин корректнее применять к наркотикам, а не к алкоголю, и в 2000 году он звучал бы анахронизмом.

Кокни называют опьянение рифмованным сленгом *BRAHMS* (от *«Brahms and Liszt»*), а фамилия Лист рифмуется с... ну, вы и сами прекрасно знаете, с чем она рифмуется в английском (*pissed*)!

Другие выражения для тяжёлого состояния опьянения — *«Paralytic»* («парализованный»), *«Blind Drunk»* («пьяный вслепую / в доску») и *«Dead Drunk»* («мертвецки пьяный») — говорят сами за себя. Интересным словом в этом ряду является *«Sozzled»* («поддатый») — диалектное словечко, означающее «неряшливо смешивать», что может характеризовать как поведение выпивохи, так и процесс приготовления пойла, доведшего его до такой кондиции.

*«Lit-up»* («озарённый, подсвеченный»), вероятно, намекает на румянец на физиономии перебравшего гражданина; *«Pie-eyed»* («ошалелый, вылупивший глаза») — забавное описание бессмысленного, остекленевшего взгляда пьяного человека. Отличной иллюстрацией этого для меня послужила фотография футбольной сборной Англии во время попойки в Гонконге: Paul Gascoigne и Teddy Sherringham выглядели совершенно *«pie-eyed»*.

*«Pickled»* («замаринованный»), скорее всего, указывает на помрачение рассудка, как и *«sloshed»* или *«smashed»*, а вот *«Stinko»* или *«Stinking»* («вонючий / до одури пьяный») обязаны своим происхождением невыносимому перегару или запаху спиртного от одежды гуляки.

Все вышеперечисленные словечки использовал Hubert Gregg, написавший в 1944 году песню о том, как он собирается отпраздновать окончание войны. Она называлась *«I'm Going to Get Lit-up When the Lights Go Up in London»* («Я напьюсь, когда в Лондоне зажгутся огни»), и в каждом куплете использовалось новое слово или выражение для одного и того же действия: например, *«I'm Going to get Pie-eyed...»*, *«I'm Going to get Pickled...»*, *«I'm Going to get Stinking...»* и так далее.

Песня приобрела колоссальную популярность, и дело дошло даже до обсуждения в Палате общин. Трезвенница Lady Astor всерьёз беспокоилась, что призывы мистера Gregg могут спровоцировать «повальный разгул и разврат», на что Winston Churchill ответил (вероятно, не без иронии): «Я уверен, что британский народ проявит похвальную сдержанность во время всенародного ликования».

И ещё одна деталь. В самом начале этого очерка я обмолвился, что, возможно, был «слегка пьян» лишь однажды в жизни. Если вы сгораете от любопытства (или даже если нет), я поведаю вам, что сие знаменательное событие произошло в ночь на 17 октября 1951 года. Это было накануне начала моей злополучной службы в армии по призыву (National Service), и коллеги по работе повели меня в местный паб «пропустить по кружке», следуя давней традиции. В конце концов, это же была пиворазливочная компания!

Не могу сказать, что вечер доставил мне массу удовольствия, но отчётливо помню, как управляющий конторой и кассир поглощали в невероятных количествах Guinness и Brown Ale, отправившись по домам изрядно потрёпанными. Сам я, полагаю, выпил пару бокалов Worthington Green Shields — исключительно из чувства приличия и чтобы хоть как-то заглушить тревожные мысли о том, что ждёт меня завтра.

Когда посиделки закончились и все с шумом разбрелись по South Lambeth Road, один из моих коллег, Freddie Clarke, не так давно сам отслуживший армейский срок, настоял на том, чтобы поехать со мной на автобусе до Camberwell и буквально довести меня до дверей дома. С его стороны это было весьма благородно, а когда я спросил, зачем он так утруждает себя, он лишь бросил: «Нельзя, чтобы завтра ты опоздал на построение, сынок», — и растворился в темноте.

**Bryan Russell**
